description: Cross-language parity for JSON Schema keyword handling at the validation boundary (spec §4.15, JSON Schema 2020-12 §6 validation keywords, §10.2/§10.3 applicators and §11 unevaluated locations).

driver_contract.path: MUST drive the same code path module invocation uses, i.e. the SDK's schema-to-native conversion followed by its validator — apcore-python generate_model() + model_validate(strict=True), apcore-typescript jsonSchemaToTypeBox() + SchemaValidator.validate(), apcore-rust validate_against_schema().
driver_contract.rationale: An earlier generation of these fixtures drove only the raw-JSON-Schema validator (validate_schema_dict / Draft202012Validator). That path is not what a module call goes through, so an entire class of converter defects — dropped type members, discarded combinator siblings, vanished array constraints — was invisible to conformance for several releases. Driving the conversion is the whole point of this file.
driver_contract.coercion: The module-invocation boundary performs NO type coercion, in any SDK, under any host configuration (TYPE_MAPPING §17.3): a contract that declares `integer` receives an integer, and `"42"` is a type error. Drivers MUST run the boundary in that mode — apcore-python `model_validate(strict=True)`, apcore-typescript `new SchemaValidator(false)`, apcore-rust `validate_against_schema()`. "No coercion" is about instance TYPES, not renderings: `4.0` still satisfies `integer` (§6.1.1 — any number with a zero fractional part) and `42` still satisfies `number`. An SDK that exposes a `coerce_types` library knob may keep it, but it MUST NOT reach this path, and it is NOT a configuration-file setting. Cases that deliberately exercise the opt-in coercing mode live in schema_validation.json.

test_cases.description: A `type` array is a union of all its members, not just the first.
apexe emits this for a value-optional flag. Collapsing to the first member rejected `true`.
An object/array member with no scalar mapping must not widen the union to accept-anything.
A numeric bound must not apply to the string branch: 5 fails `minimum: 10`.
What apexe emits for `ls --color[=WHEN]`.
An enum member outside the declared types is still rejected by the type half.
`type` and a combinator are independent assertions; both must hold (§10.2).
Not just the first one found: the `not` here excludes an otherwise valid enum member.
`const`/`enum` members may be any JSON value, not only scalars.
§6.4.2. Array option keywords were dropped wholesale by at least one converter.
The array branch of a `type` array must carry the array keywords.
§6.4.4/§6.4.5: minContains/maxContains are inert without `contains`. Emitting them bare turns this into a schema that rejects every array.
Distinct instance types. `bool` subclasses `int` in Python, which made lax coercion read `true` as `1`.
The guard must not stop a genuine boolean branch from claiming the value.
A shallow type mapping widened array/object/bare-constraint sub-schemas to accept-anything.
§7.2.1: an unrecognised format MUST NOT be treated as an assertion failure. apexe#32.
SHOULD-level: the SDK may warn, but validation passes. The warning itself is covered by schema_hardening_formats.json.
§10.3.1.1 — each prefix position is validated against its own sub-schema.
Only positions that exist are constrained; `minItems` is what asserts length.
§10.3.1.2 — with `prefixItems` present, `items` describes only the tail. Applying it to the whole array rejected this valid instance.
An array applicator on a type-less schema must not narrow the accepted instance type.
§10.3.2.2 — a key matching the pattern is validated against its sub-schema.
§10.3.2.3 — a pattern-matched key is not `additional`, so `additionalProperties: false` must not reject it.
§10.3.2.4 — the sub-schema is applied to each key string, not to its value.
§6.5.4 — the trigger key's presence requires its dependents.
Applicators on the root schema must be enforced too, not only on property sub-schemas.
§10.2.2.4 — the trigger key applies a whole sub-schema to the object.
§10.2.2.1/§10.2.2.2 — `if` asserts nothing itself; it selects `then`.
§10.2.2.3 — a failing `if` selects `else`.
`if` alone produces annotations only; it never fails an instance.
§11.3 — `z` is reached by no applicator, so `unevaluatedProperties: false` rejects it.
The annotation from the `allOf` member is what makes `a` evaluated — a plain `additionalProperties: false` would reject it.
The `then` branch is not applied when `if` fails, so `extra` stays unevaluated.
§11.2 — `prefixItems` evaluated index 0 only, so index 1 is unevaluated.
§10.3.1.3 — `contains` evaluates exactly the positions that matched it.
`{required: [...]}` is a complete schema and is what if/then/dependentSchemas sub-schemas usually look like; dropping it made every such condition vacuously true.
A `$ref: "#"` re-entered through properties/items is a recursive data structure, not a cycle. Depth 1: a leaf node.
The same schema three levels deep. Resolving the reference eagerly never terminates; binding it lazily does.
The recursive position must keep asserting: widening an unresolved `$ref` to accept-anything made the whole sub-tree unchecked.
`required` inside the recursive target still applies at depth.
A document may reference itself by its own `$id` instead of by `#` — the canonical form used by schema_hardening_recursive.json.
Same `$id` self-reference, invalid at depth 2.
Recursion anchored on a `$defs` entry rather than on the document root.
The `$defs`-anchored recursive position must keep asserting at depth.
`oneOf` exclusivity is location-independent: 3 satisfies both `integer` and `number`. Mapping `oneOf` onto a host union type degrades it to `anyOf` and accepted this.
3.5 satisfies `number` only, so exactly one branch matches.
Zero matches fails just as two do.
Exclusivity applies inside `items` too, not only inside `properties`.
Same schema, a value only the `number` branch accepts.
`anyOf` has no exclusivity rule — the same input `oneOf` rejects is valid here.
`type` and `oneOf` are independent assertions (§10.2); the union half still has to be exclusive when the intersection buries it.
Only the `minimum: 0` branch matches 50, so the union half is satisfied.
A root-level combinator has no owning property; generating a field-less model for it accepted every input.
Root-level `anyOf` with neither `required` satisfied.
Root-level `anyOf` with the first branch satisfied.
`uniqueItems` over an array of objects. A hash-set implementation raised a bare TypeError here instead of failing validation.
Distinct objects satisfy `uniqueItems`.
JSON Schema object equality ignores key order, so these two members are duplicates.
`uniqueItems` over an array of arrays — the other non-hashable item type.
Element order distinguishes two otherwise equal arrays.

The module-invocation boundary performs NO type coercion (TYPE_MAPPING §17.3). `"42"` is a string instance; `integer` rejects it. A module's input contract has to mean the same thing regardless of which host loaded it, so this is not host-configurable.
Coercion is not one-directional either — a number is not a string.

§6.1.1 defines `integer` as any number with a zero fractional part, so `4.0` IS an integer. "No coercion" means no *type* coercion — it must not become "reject a JSON integer written with a decimal point".
§6.1.1: `number` matches any numeric instance, integers included. Not a coercion.
The rule holds at depth, not just on top-level properties.
An `items` sub-schema must apply the same `integer` rule a top-level property gets.
A nullable integer is still an integer — the `null` member does not open a coercion path.
`enum` compares instances, not renderings: `"2"` is not the integer `2`.
An object contract receives an object, not a JSON document to parse.
